title: The business of El Niño
description:
El Niño is expected to bring wild weather, but it's also business opportunity for some. Contractors are booked up as homeowners prepare for heavy rains and ski resorts gear up to cash in on snow.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST: It is a super El Niño year. The natural climate pattern is shaking up winter weather across the country. Some areas could be drier and warmer, others could be greater than average precipitation, and that is creating some business opportunities. NPR's Ava Berger reports on the economics of El Niño.AVA BERGER, BYLINE: Business is booming, that is, in the sump pump worlds in places where El Niño is expected to disrupt weather patterns and bring heavy rains.ARMANDO CHAN: Right now, we are running a double of the crews what we used to run, and we're trying to help as much homes that we can before the rains come.BERGER: Armando Chan, who owns a drainage company in Northern California, is getting 50 to 60 calls a day. That's compared to his average of 10. Now, some regions of the country are already getting hit with heavy rains and floods, which are made more likely and more intense by El Niño, like in the Southwest. Thousands have been forced from their homes. Several people died.THOMAS DONALDSON: That is a bedroom with - that's just all mud. But I don't think I'll ever see something like this ever in my lifetime here.BERGER: Thomas Donaldson is a co-owner of Redemption Restoration and Cleaning in Farmington, New Mexico. He and his crews have been really busy, especially Oliver.DONALDSON: So this is Oliver.BERGER: (Laughter) Oliver is a very good boy and a certified mold-sniffing dog, a German Shepherd trained to find mold that grows behind damp walls. He's booked up solid.DONALDSON: After lunchtime, he just wants to lay down and not really work. He's just like, no, I'm good. But he's got to go to work today.BERGER: El Niño also works as an advertising strategy. Shari Freeman is a property damage attorney in central Florida. She represents homeowners and insurance disputes. On her website, she's offering free insurance claim reviews. This El Niño year, parts of Florida are expected to see some of the highest levels of precipitation, and it's already started in some areas.SHARI FREEMAN: Personally, I think, you know, Floridians are generally a little lax with El Niños just because, you know, they're like, oh, it means no hurricanes. But, you know, it's definitely something that we need to be vigilant about.BERGER: Tire Supply Network's ad on YouTube is much more direct, using local news stories to raise the alarm about potential bad weather.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: ...Strongest El Niños ever recorded.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: El Niño is back.BERGER: Christopher Littlejohn is the social media manager at the national tire parts supplier based out of California. He also appears in the ad.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)CHRISTOPHER LITTLEJOHN: That's not El Niño. That's El Hombre.BERGER: His company says, compared to last year, the sale of metal tire stud setup kits has doubled. Tire studs are like cleats for car wheels to use in the snow.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)LITTLEJOHN: Because the first storm is a bad time to realize you're not ready. And if you're not ready, Tire Supply Network has your back.BERGER: Forecasters predict El Niño could bring more snow to areas of the Southwest and southern U.S. Nathan Rafferty is ready. He promotes Utah's ski resorts and has found that El Niño makes for a great campaign slogan, even though the midterms are over.NATHAN RAFFERTY: Vote super El Niño in '26, '27, the greatest snow on Earth. It's a candidate we can all get behind.BERGER: It began as a joke to get people excited about the coming ski season, but it's caught on as a slogan on yard signs and T-shirts in and around Salt Lake City.RAFFERTY: The yard signs are just really tongue in cheek. We are hoping for snowmageddon. Nothing would make me happier.BERGER: An El Niño economy is real, and it's just getting started.Ava Berger, NPR News. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved.
